ECE 6612

CSRF, CORS and action intent

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows a browser carrying session credentials into an action request and a server deciding whether to accept it.

A logged-in account page lets its user change a delivery address. A session cookie identifies the account. If an attacker can cause that browser to submit a chosen address and the server accepts the request, the account changes even though the attacker never learned the session value. Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) exploits the browser’s role as a credential-carrying deputy.

Trace a CSRF case through its inputs: an action the attacker can induce, attacker-chosen action data, an active victim session, and credentials that the browser actually sends. The request method, encoding, site relationship, cookie SameSite policy and request credential mode all matter. State-changing GET handlers can expose actions to ordinary link or image loading. Sensitive operations should use appropriate methods plus explicit intent checks.

A synchronizer token is an unpredictable value associated with the session that the legitimate page can supply and the server verifies for an action. It must reach the correct validation point and resist attacker acquisition. Origin validation compares a browser-supplied request origin with a trusted allowlist; missing or unexpected values require an explicit policy. A carefully designed SameSite cookie policy reduces cross-site credential delivery. These controls protect different stages and can work together.

CORS, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, grants a script permission to read selected cross-origin response data. A server can return Access-Control-Allow-Origin for a specific requesting origin. Credentialed reading also requires the matching credential permission; a wildcard origin does not grant credentialed sharing. Some methods, headers or content types require a preflight request. Simple cross-origin requests, such as eligible form submissions, can reach the server without that preflight.

The Same-Origin Policy and CORS govern browser access to response information. The server’s CSRF and authorization checks decide whether an action should happen. An attacker can benefit from an accepted action while the browser hides the reply. Conversely, a permitted cross-origin reader still needs the application’s authorization for the requested resource.

For window messaging, postMessage lets a sender specify an intended target origin. The receiver checks event.origin, the expected source window and the message structure before acting. A correct origin check identifies the communicating document; authorization then decides which actions that document may request. XSS within a trusted page can use the page’s readable tokens and authority, which makes safe page execution part of the larger action boundary.

Example

A picture-hosting page induces a form POST to a billing site. Assume the browser sends the billing session cookie and the handler accepts a new address with no token or origin check. The change can succeed even while SOP hides the billing response from the picture page. Adding a session-bound token that the picture page cannot obtain gives the billing handler a concrete intent check.

Sources and scope
  • C15 Web Basics: SOP, CORS and postMessage; C16 Web Security: CSRF defenses.
  • WHATWG Fetch: CORS checks, request credentials and preflight.
  • WHATWG HTML: cross-document messaging and origin checks.

Practice

1. An attacker page can submit a simple cross-origin POST, but CORS prevents it from reading the reply. The target accepts the victim’s cookie and updates the account without a CSRF token. Can the update occur? Explain the stages.

Separate delivering the request, validating the action and exposing the response.

Yes. The browser can deliver an eligible simple POST with the permitted credentials. The target then accepts the action using the session. CORS can withhold the reply from attacker JavaScript after the state change. The target needs an action-intent check such as a correctly validated session-bound token and an appropriate origin/cookie policy.

2. A cookie has SameSite=Strict. A request comes from a compromised sibling subdomain over the same scheme. Which boundary must you evaluate before relying on Strict as the action defense?

Compare origin and registrable-domain site boundaries.

A sibling subdomain has a different origin but can share the same site. SameSite=Strict governs cross-site delivery, so a same-site sibling request may remain eligible. The server still needs its intended origin and action checks, and the actual request’s credential behavior must be traced.
